meta.title: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce service?
meta.subtitle: Board discussion document on Parcelbird Now
meta.purpose: Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery service in three Midwest cities, in 2027, and reach profit within its $12.0M cash?
meta.confidentiality: Synthetic benchmark data: the company, competitors and figures are fictional

inputs.label: Parcelbird board briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data)
Choices made without the user (unavailable during the work)
inputs.content: Mode deck_deep (board decision); material = briefing pack only; audience = board, approve or reject; theme navy; deck type client diagnostic, 30–40 slides; $9.5M read as covering all company spending to month 18 (the reading kinder to the plan); contribution per order shown before and after site fixed costs.

problem.statement: Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery service in three Midwest cities, in 2027, and reach profit within its $12.0M cash?
problem.decision_maker: The board: two founders and two investors
success_criteria: A path to profitability within the current $12.0M cash, with no new round
At least 12 months of runway at all times
No harm to the growth of the software business
problem.accuracy: Order of magnitude: enough to tell profit from loss per order and to test the runway rule

one_day_answer.situation: Parcelbird sells dark-store software growing 60% a year and holds $12.0M of cash
one_day_answer.complication: The founders want to operate stores, but stores on our own software lose money per order and the plan needs more cash than the runway rule allows
one_day_answer.resolution: Decline the launch in 2027 and sell fast delivery from grocers' own stores as software instead

storyline.governing_thought: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; sell fast delivery to grocers as software instead
